opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was something we went back and forth on quite a bit. The core question we were trying to answer was pretty practical: if you take labels generated by a foundation model, zero-shot, and use them to train a smaller, task-specific model, how does that downstream model compare to one trained on human-annotated labels? And the answer to that question really depends on what you're training downstream, so we couldn't just pick one architecture and call it a day.

So we deliberately chose models that reflect what people actually deploy. In practice, most teams aren't shipping a giant open-vocabulary detector to an edge device or running it at scale in production; they're training something like a YOLO-family model, or a more conventional detector, something efficient and well understood. Those were the natural targets, because the whole value proposition of auto-labeling is that you use the big, expensive model once, offline, to produce the labels, and then you train the lean model you'll actually run.

We also wanted some diversity, so we weren't measuring the quirks of one particular network. Different architectures respond differently to label noise. Some are more forgiving of slightly loose bounding boxes, others are more sensitive to missed objects or false positives in the training data. Auto-generated labels have a characteristic error profile: they tend to be confident, they can miss small or unusual objects, and the box tightness can differ from what a careful human annotator would draw. So we wanted to see whether the conclusions held across models, not just for one.

And then there was a controllability piece. We tried to keep the training recipe as fixed as possible: same splits, same schedules, same evaluation protocol, so the only real variable was where the labels came from and things like the confidence threshold we used to filter them. That threshold turned out to be one of the more interesting knobs, actually. People's intuition is often to keep only the highest-confidence labels, but a fairly moderate threshold often worked better, because you trade a bit of precision for a lot more recall in the training set, and the downstream model can tolerate some noise.

The broad takeaway was encouraging: for a lot of common categories, models trained on auto-labels got surprisingly close to models trained on human labels, at a tiny fraction of the cost and time. But it wasn't uniform. For rare classes, fine-grained distinctions, or domains far from what the foundation model saw in pretraining, humans still matter a lot. So I'd frame it less as "replace annotation" and more as "auto-label first, then spend your human effort where the model is uncertain or wrong."

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was something we debated quite a bit internally, because there's a real tension there. On one hand, you want to use the architectures that practitioners actually deploy, because the whole point of the study is to ask whether auto-labels are good enough to train the models people care about. On the other hand, if you pick a single architecture, you're always open to the critique that the result is an artifact of that one model's inductive biases.

So we ended up spanning a range. For the detection and segmentation experiments we used a mix of what I'd call the workhorse models, things in the YOLO and DETR families, plus a couple of convolutional backbones that have been around long enough that everyone understands their behavior. And we deliberately included models at different capacity levels, because one of the questions we had going in was whether larger models are more or less forgiving of label noise. The intuition people have is that a bigger model can "see through" noisy labels, and I wanted to actually test that rather than assume it.

The other principle was that we didn't want the downstream model to be the same model, or even the same family, as the auto-labeler. If you auto-label with a large vision-language model and then train a student that shares a lot of architectural DNA with it, you can get a kind of circularity where the student just learns to reproduce the teacher's mistakes very fluently, and the metrics look fine. Keeping some distance between the labeling model and the downstream model gave us a cleaner read on whether the labels themselves carried useful signal.

And frankly, we kept the training recipes pretty vanilla. No clever noise-robust losses, no label-smoothing tricks tuned for this setting. If the auto-labels only work when you wrap them in a specialized training procedure, that's a different claim than "you can swap these in for human labels," and we wanted to be honest about which claim we were making.

astra-6.text:
We wanted to separate two questions: how good are the labels, and how much does the downstream architecture affect what you can learn from those labels? If you change both at once, it becomes difficult to attribute the result.

So the way I’d frame the comparison is to hold the downstream model and training procedure fixed, and compare training on human annotations with training on automatically generated annotations. Then, across architectures, you can ask whether that relationship holds. Does the auto-labeled data remain useful, or is the benefit specific to a particular model?

The goal isn’t necessarily to find the architecture that gives you the highest number. It’s to understand whether the labels are useful for training the model you actually want to deploy.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted to understand whether the automatically generated labels were useful beyond one particular model. If you generate labels with one architecture and then train that same architecture on them, it’s hard to separate the quality of the labels from the biases of the model. So the idea was to look at downstream architectures as a way to test that transfer: can a different model learn something useful from these labels? The architecture choice was secondary to that question. What we cared about was how well the resulting model performed, rather than just how plausible the annotations looked.
